central_claim: Two registries read on two snapshot dates show that trial eligibility is often written on a molecular/fusion class while the registry's searchable 'listed conditions' field names histologies, so a condition search on a patient's own EMC diagnosis misses recruiting trials that would in fact admit them, and that a keyword-based fix (rather than reading eligibility text trial-by-trial) would introduce costly false positives.

p1s.summary: Section 1's mechanism explanation includes an unhedged, uncited comparative claim about common cancers ('for a common cancer the two coincide, so nobody notices') that the paper's own evidence base -- an audit confined to an ultra-rare fusion-driven sarcoma across two registries -- never measures and cannot support. It is stated as settled fact rather than as speculation, and it is not even clearly true in general: molecularly-defined trials in common cancers (e.g. biomarker-selected basket/umbrella designs) can exhibit the identical listed-conditions/eligibility-criteria mismatch this paper describes for EMC, so the sentence risks readers taking a plausible-sounding but unaudited generalization as part of the paper's demonstrated finding.
p1s.evidence: research/manuscripts/care-delivery/emc-trial-reachability.md, Section 1 ('The mechanism'), line: 'For a common cancer the two coincide, so nobody notices.' No registry data on common-cancer trials appears anywhere in the document; the scope frontmatter and Sections 2-5 describe retrieval scoped entirely to EMC/FET-fusion-sarcoma-related searches on two registries (ClinicalTrials.gov and one non-US registry).
p1s.fix: Either hedge the sentence to mark it as an unaudited illustrative premise (e.g. 'For a common cancer the two fields may more often coincide by construction, though this audit did not test that -- so nobody notices') or delete it and let the two-field mechanism stand on its own without the common-cancer contrast, since the contrast is not load-bearing for the rest of the argument.
